extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers studying political economy, trade and agricultural policy (readers of Adam Smith / Wealth of Nations)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for classifying labour, expenses, and policy effects on national wealth — especially distinctions between proprietors, cultivators, and artificers/manufacturers/merchants, and policy prescriptions about trade and land improvement. Useful for evaluating economic policy effects on agricultural production and national revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productive and unproductive classes (Quesnai's three classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The different orders of people are divided into three classes: proprietors of land; cultivators (farmers and country labourers), called the productive class; artificers, manufacturers, and merchants, called the barren or unproductive class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the classificatory standard used by the French system (Quesnai) to analyze how the annual produce of land and labour is distributed among social classes; subsequent discussion evaluates and critiques this classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of productive expenses (original and annual expenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The cultivators' original and annual expenses (depenses primitives, et depenses annuelles) consist of instruments of husbandry, stock of cattle, seed, and maintenance of the farmer’s family/servants/cattle until returns begin; and annual expenses are seed, wear-and-tear, and maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two sorts of expenses are capitals the farmer employs in cultivation and must be regularly restored together with a reasonable profit; the portion of produce necessary to replace these is 'a fund sacred to cultivation' — if landlords violate it (by excessive rent), they diminish future produce and rents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground expenses (landlord improvements) treated as productive
rubrics_metrics.description: The ground expenses which the proprietor lays out upon improvement of land (buildings, drains, inclosures, ameliorations) are called ground expenses (depenses foncieres) and considered productive because, once repaid with ordinary profits, they occasion a reproduction of a neat produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until repaid, the advanced rent attributable to these ground expenses ought to be regarded as sacred and inviolable (not subject to tithe or taxation), because taxing them discourages improvement and thus future tithes/taxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper definition of rent (neat produce after necessary expenses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rent which properly belongs to the landlord is the neat produce which remains after paying, in the completest manner, all the necessary expenses previously laid out to raise the whole produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rent should be no more than this remainder; extracting more undermines cultivation and ultimately reduces the landlord's own future rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for labours being productive: does labour add to annual produce?
rubrics_metrics.description: In Quesnai's system, 'productive' labour is that which adds to the annual produce of the land (e.g., cultivators produce neat produce/rent); 'unproductive' labour (artificers/manufacturers/merchants) is said to replace only the stock which employs them together with ordinary profits and not to increase the sum total of the rude produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith critiques this: even if an artificer’s consumption equals his production over a period, his work fixes vendible commodities and increases the actually existing market value at moments in time; classification should consider whether the work fixes value and enables exchange, not only instantaneous net addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between artificers/manufacturers and menial servants
rubrics_metrics.description: Menial servants' services perish at the instant of performance and do not fix themselves in vendible commodities; artificers and manufacturers produce vendible commodities which fix and realize value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore artificers and manufacturers should not be equated with barren menial servants; this is a criterion for classifying labour productive/unproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prohibiting agricultural exports (policy criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibiting the exportation of corn and excluding the inhabitants of the country from foreign markets discouraged and kept down agriculture in France below its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy that excludes rural producers from foreign markets, or imposes restraints/taxes on transport between provinces, will depress agricultural production and reduce national produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of trade as the most effectual expedient
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect freedom of trade (allowing foreign merchants, artificers, and manufacturers free trade) is the most effectual method for a landed nation to raise up its own artificers, manufacturers, and merchants and to raise the value of the surplus produce of its land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing foreign competition raises the value of agricultural surplus, creates capital, and over time fosters domestic manufactures more advantageously than protectionist duties or prohibitions; restrictive duties sink the real value of surplus produce and discourage agriculture.

rubrics_metrics.name: How duties and prohibitions harm landed nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppressing foreign trade by high duties or prohibitions raises the price of foreign goods and sinks the real value of the surplus produce of the land, and by giving monopoly to home manufacturers raises mercantile/manufacturing profit relative to agricultural profit, drawing capital away from agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such policy discourages agriculture both by lowering its returns and by diverting capital to other employments; premature encouragement of manufactures can depress more valuable productive labour (agriculture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms by which artificers/manufacturers can augment national wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificers, manufacturers, and merchants can augment the revenue and wealth of society only by parsimony (saving) — they annually reproduce only the funds destined for their subsistence unless they save part of that revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Savings out of their revenue increase capital available for augmenting useful labour; without saving their industry alone does not increase the annual produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two ways to augment annual produce (criterion for growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual produce of any society can be augmented only either by improvement in the productive powers of useful labour (better ability and machinery) or by increase in the quantity of that labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements in productive powers are especially available to manufacturing labour (due to greater subdivision of labour); increase in quantity of useful labour depends on increase of capital, which equals savings from revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural distribution and effects of encroachment (policy consequence criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr Quesnai's 'Economical Table' represents a natural distribution under perfect liberty; any encroachment (favouring proprietors or the barren class) that violates that natural distribution will necessarily degrade the value and sum total of the annual produce and occasion a gradual declension in real wealth and revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of decline corresponds to degree of violation; policy should avoid systematic encroachment on the productive class' share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainability condition for farmers (replacement of capitals and profits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The part of produce remaining to a farmer after paying rent ought to be sufficient first to replace within a reasonable time the whole of his original expenses together with the ordinary profits of stock, and secondly to replace annually the whole of his annual expenses together with ordinary profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these two capitals are not regularly restored with profit, the farmer cannot continue and will abandon cultivation — rents and policies must allow these replacements to sustain agriculture.
